translation_en: Uqbah ibn Amir reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “The expiation for a vow is the same as the expiation for an oath.” The transmitters include Harun ibn Said, Yunus ibn Abd al-Ala, Ahmad ibn Isa, Ibn Wahb, Amr ibn al-Harith, Kab ibn Alqamah, Abd al-Rahman ibn Shumasah, Abu al-Khayr, and Uqbah.

Umar ibn al-Khattab reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Allah forbids you to swear by your fathers.” Umar said, “By Allah, since I heard the Messenger of Allah forbid it, I have never sworn by them, whether deliberately or while repeating someone else.” The chain is Abu Tahir and Harmalah from Ibn Wahb and Yunus, through Ibn Shihab, Salim, and Ibn Umar.

This is the same report from Umar through al-Zuhri, in the chains of Uqayl, Abd al-Razzaq, and Maamar. Uqayl’s version says Umar never swore by them or spoke such an oath, and omits the phrase “deliberately or while repeating someone else.” The alternate transmitters are Abd al-Malik ibn Shuayb, his father and grandfather, Uqayl, Abd al-Razzaq, and Maamar, all reporting the same ruling from al-Zuhri.

Ibn Umar reported that the Prophet heard Umar swear by his father. This is similar to Yunus’s and Maamar’s reports. The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Amr al-Naqid, and Zuhayr ibn Harb from Sufyan ibn Uyaynah, al-Zuhri, Salim, and his father.

Ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah came upon Umar among a group of travelers while Umar was swearing by his father. The Messenger called out: “Allah forbids you to swear by your fathers. Whoever swears an oath should swear by Allah or remain silent.” The chain is Qutaybah ibn Said and Muhammad ibn Rumh from al-Layth, Nafi, and Abdullah, who reported it from the Messenger.

This story is transmitted through several chains from Nafi and Ibn Umar, including Ubayd Allah, Ayyub, al-Walid ibn Kathir, Ismail ibn Umayyah, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Dhib, Abd al-Razzaq, and Ibn Jurayj, with wording like the preceding narration. The report comes through Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Numayr, Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, Yahya al-Qattan, Ubayd Allah, Bishr ibn Hilal, Abd al-Warith, Ayyub, Abu Kurayb, Abu Usamah, al-Walid ibn Kathir, Ibn Abi Umar, Sufyan, Ismail ibn Umayyah, Ibn Rafi, Ibn Abi Fudayk, al-Dahhak, Ibn Abi Dhib, Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jurayj, and Abd al-Karim, all from Nafi and Ibn Umar, with the same story.

Ibn Umar reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath should swear only by Allah.” Quraysh used to swear by their fathers, so the Prophet said: “Do not swear by your fathers.” Quraysh used to swear by their fathers, so the Prophet forbade it. This report is transmitted by Yahya ibn Yahya, Yahya ibn Ayyub, Qutaybah, and Ibn Hujr through Ismail ibn Jafar, Abdullah ibn Dinar, and Ibn Umar.

Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “If any of you swears by al-Lat, let him say, ‘There is no god but Allah.’ If anyone says to his companion, ‘Come, let us gamble,’ let him give charity.” The report is transmitted through Abu Tahir and Harmalah from Ibn Wahb, Yunus, Ibn Shihab, and Humayd ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, from Abu Hurairah.

This is the same report through al-Zuhri. Maamar’s version says, “Let him give something in charity,” and al-Awzai’s says, “Whoever swears by al-Lat and al-Uzza.” Muslim noted that the wording about inviting someone to gamble and then giving charity is reported only by al-Zuhri, who has about ninety soundly transmitted reports from the Prophet with no other narrator sharing them. This is the same chain through Suwayd ibn Said, al-Walid ibn Muslim, and al-Awzai; and through Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, Abd ibn Humayd, Abd al-Razzaq, and Maamar. Maamar says, “Let him give something in charity”; al-Awzai says, “Whoever swears by al-Lat and al-Uzza.” Muslim notes this unusual wording about gambling is reported only by al-Zuhri.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Do not swear by false gods or by your fathers.” The chain is Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd al-Ala, Hisham, al-Hasan, and Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah.

Abu Musa al-Ashari said: “I came to the Prophet with a group of Asharis asking him for mounts. He said, ‘By Allah, I cannot provide mounts for you; I have nothing to carry you on.’ We waited as long as Allah willed. Then some camels were brought, and he gave us three fine, high-backed camels. As we set out, we said that Allah would not bless us: we had come asking for mounts, the Messenger swore he would not give us any, yet he then gave us mounts. We went back and told him. He said, ‘I did not carry you; Allah carried you. By Allah, whenever I swear an oath and then see something better, I will offer expiation for my oath and do what is better, if Allah wills.’”

Abu Musa said his companions sent him to ask the Messenger for mounts while they were with him on the expedition of hardship, Tabuk. Abu Musa found the Prophet angry and heard him swear that he would not provide anything. He returned distressed, fearing the Prophet was upset with him. A short while later Bilal called him, saying the Messenger wanted him. The Prophet gave him six camels he had just bought from Sad and told him to take them to his companions, saying Allah—or the Messenger—would provide them as mounts. Abu Musa did so, but insisted that some companions accompany him to confirm what the Prophet had said and that he had not invented the account. They believed him and went with him to those who had heard the Prophet first refuse and then provide the camels; they confirmed Abu Musa’s account exactly. Abu Musa said that during the expedition of hardship, the campaign of Tabuk, his companions sent him to ask for mounts. He found the Messenger in a state of anger and heard him swear he would provide nothing. Abu Musa feared the Prophet was displeased with him. After returning to his companions, Bilal called him back to the Messenger, who gave him six camels he had just purchased from Sad and instructed him to carry his companions on them. Abu Musa made the companions verify this account with those who had heard the initial refusal and later provision; they confirmed it exactly. The transmitters are Abdullah ibn Barrad and Muhammad ibn al-Ala through Abu Usamah, Burayd, Abu Burdah, and Abu Musa.

Zahdam al-Jarmi said they were with Abu Musa, who had a meal of chicken. A man from Banu Taym Allah, with a reddish complexion resembling a non-Arab, entered. Abu Musa invited him to eat. The man hesitated, so Abu Musa said he had seen the Messenger of Allah eat chicken. The man said he had seen something about it that made him dislike it, and had sworn not to eat it. Abu Musa said: “Let me tell you about that. I came to the Messenger with a group of Asharis asking for mounts. He swore he could not provide any. After we waited, camels from a raid were brought to him, and he gave us five fine camels. As we left, we worried that we had overlooked his oath and would not be blessed. We returned and asked whether he had forgotten swearing not to provide mounts. He said, ‘By Allah, whenever I swear an oath and then see that something else is better, I do what is better and offer expiation for my oath. Go, for Allah Almighty provided these mounts for you.’”

This is a similar report from Zahdam al-Jarmi through Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, Ayyub, Abu Qilabah, and al-Qasim al-Tamimi. It notes the friendship between this branch of Jarm and the Asharis and that chicken was served to Abu Musa.

This is the same account through other chains from Zahdam: Ismail ibn Ulayyah and Ayyub; Sufyan and Abu Qilabah; and Wuhayb with Ayyub, Abu Qilabah, and al-Qasim. They report the story with the meaning of Hammad ibn Zayd’s narration. These are alternate chains from Zahdam al-Jarmi: Ali ibn Hujr, Ishaq ibn Ibrahim, and Ibn Numayr through Ismail ibn Ulayyah and Ayyub; Ibn Abi Umar through Sufyan and Ayyub; and Abu Bakr ibn Ishaq through Affan, Wuhayb, and Ayyub. They all tell the account with the meaning of Hammad ibn Zayd’s report.

Zahdam al-Jarmi said he visited Abu Musa while he was eating chicken and related a similar account. This version adds that Abu Musa said, “By Allah, I had not forgotten my oath.” Zahdam said he entered upon Abu Musa while he was eating chicken. This report follows the same story and adds that Abu Musa said, “By Allah, I had not forgotten the oath.” It is transmitted through Shayban ibn Farrukh, al-Saq, Matar al-Warraq, and Zahdam.

Abu Musa al-Ashari said: “We came to the Messenger of Allah asking for mounts. He said, ‘I have nothing to carry you on; by Allah, I cannot provide mounts.’ Then he sent us three camels with white patches on their backs. We told him that we had come asking for mounts, he had sworn not to provide them, and then he had sent them. He said, ‘Whenever I swear an oath and then see something better, I do what is better.’”

Abu Musa reported that they were on foot and came to the Prophet asking for mounts. This is similar to Jarir’s report. Abu Musa said they were walking and came to the Prophet asking for mounts. This is similar to Jarir’s report and comes through Muhammad ibn Abd al-Ala, al-Mutamir, his father, Abu al-Salil, and Zahdam.

Abu Hurairah said a man stayed late with the Prophet, then returned home and found his children asleep. His family brought him food, but he swore he would not eat because of his children. Later he changed his mind and ate. He told the Messenger of Allah, who said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees that something else is better should do what is better and offer expiation for his oath.”

Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees that something else is better should offer expiation for his oath and do what is better.” Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better should offer expiation for the oath and do what is better.” This chain is Abu Tahir, Abdullah ibn Wahb, Malik, Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, his father, and Abu Hurairah.

This is the same report through Zuhayr ibn Harb, Ibn Abi Uways, Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Muttalib, Suhayl ibn Abi Salih, his father, and Abu Hurairah. The Prophet said to do what is better and offer expiation for the oath. Abu Hurairah reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better should do what is better and offer expiation for the oath.” The transmitters are Zuhayr ibn Harb, Ibn Abi Uways, Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Muttalib, Suhayl, his father, and Abu Hurairah.

This report comes through al-Qasim ibn Zakariyya, Khalid ibn Makhlad, Sulayman ibn Bilal, and Suhayl, with the meaning of Malik’s narration: “Let him offer expiation for his oath and do what is better.”

A man asked Adi ibn Hatim for help paying the price of a servant. Adi said he had only his armor and helmet to offer, and could write to his family to give them to the man. The man was not satisfied, so Adi became angry and swore he would give him nothing. The man then accepted. Adi said: “By Allah, had I not heard the Messenger of Allah say, ‘Whoever swears an oath and then sees something more mindful of Allah, let him do what is more mindful of Allah,’ I would not have broken my oath.”

Adi ibn Hatim reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something else that is better should do what is better and leave his oath.” Adi ibn Hatim reported that the Messenger of Allah said: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better should do what is better and leave the oath.” The chain is Ubayd Allah ibn Muadh, his father, Shubah, Abd al-Aziz ibn Rafi, and Tamim ibn Tarafah.

Adi ibn Hatim reported that the Prophet said: “If any of you swears an oath and then sees something better, let him offer expiation for it and do what is better.” Adi ibn Hatim reported that the Prophet said: “If any of you swears an oath and then sees something better, let him offer expiation and do what is better.” This is transmitted through Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn Numayr and Muhammad ibn Tarif, from Muhammad ibn Fudayl, al-Amash, Abd al-Aziz ibn Rafi, and Tamim al-Tai.
Adi ibn Hatim heard the Prophet say the same. This is transmitted through Muhammad ibn Tarif, Muhammad ibn Fudayl, al-Shaybani, Abd al-Aziz ibn Rafi, and Tamim al-Tai.

Tamim ibn Tarafah said he heard Adi ibn Hatim refuse a man who asked him for one hundred dirhams. Adi said, “You ask me for one hundred dirhams when I am the son of Hatim? By Allah, I will not give it to you.” Then he recalled hearing the Messenger of Allah say: “Whoever swears an oath and then sees something better should do what is better.”

This is the same account through Muhammad ibn Hatim, Bahz, Shubah, and Simak ibn Harb. It adds Adi’s words to the man: “You have four hundred in my stipend.” This is the same account through Muhammad ibn Hatim, Bahz, Shubah, Simak ibn Harb, Tamim ibn Tarafah, and Adi ibn Hatim. The report adds that the man would receive four hundred from Adi’s stipend.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah said the Messenger of Allah told him: “Do not ask for leadership. If it is granted to you because you asked for it, you will be left to manage it on your own; if it is granted without your asking, you will be helped in it. If you swear an oath and then see that something else is better, offer expiation for your oath and do what is better.” The Messenger of Allah told Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah not to ask for leadership: if it is given because he asked, he will be left to manage it alone; if it is given without his asking, he will be helped. He also told him that if he swears an oath and later sees something better, he should offer expiation and do what is better. The transmitters are Shayban ibn Farrukh, Jarir ibn Hazim, al-Hasan, and Abd al-Rahman.

This is the same report through several chains from al-Hasan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah. Ali ibn Hujr reports through Hushaim, Yunus, Mansur, and Humayd; Abu Kamil through Hammad ibn Zayd, Simak ibn Atiyyah, Yunus ibn Ubayd, and Hisham ibn Hassan; and others through al-Mutamir, his father, Said, and Qatadah. The chain of al-Mutamir’s report omits the words about leadership. This is the same hadith through several chains from al-Hasan and Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah. The transmitters include Ali ibn Hujr, Hushaim, Yunus, Mansur, and Humayd; Abu Kamil, Hammad ibn Zayd, Simak ibn Atiyyah, Yunus ibn Ubayd, and Hisham ibn Hassan; and Ubayd Allah ibn Muadh and al-Mutamir. The version through al-Mutamir and his father does not mention leadership.
